This message comes from Schwab.
Investing with Schwab is like a hike with endless trails.
Go solo with self-directed investing,
take stops along the way with trading,
or choose a guide with full service wealth management.
Whatever trails you take,
you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington,
I'm Corva Coleman.
Today is the first day for President Trump's new Chief of Staff, Stephen Miller.
NPR's Mara Lison reports Miller is known for his confrontational style.
Trump said one of the reasons he chose him is because Miller is "a fighter and very loyal."
And here is Miller talking last year about crime in Memphis, Tennessee.
The gangbangers that you deal with,
they think that they're ruthless.
They have no idea how ruthless we are.
They think they're tough.
They have no idea how tough.
We are.
They think that they're hardcore.
We are so much more hardcore than they are.
And we have the entire weight of the United States government behind us.
But just last night, Trump said in a 60 Minutes interview on CBS
that his administration's deportation policy may have gone too far.
NPR's Mara Lison reporting.
Israel's president has tapped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main rival,
Gadi Isincut, to try to form the next Israeli government.
And NPR's Lauren Freya reports today is Isincut's first full day of coalition-building efforts.
Center-right Gadi Isincut won slightly fewer votes in last month's Israeli election
than his rival incumbent Prime Minister Netanyahu on the far right.
But neither won a majority, and more of the other political parties want Isincut to govern.
In a ceremony at the president's office...
We have no idea where we are.
Isincut said his door is open to coalition partners.
But that anyone who tries to thwart coalition-building for personal reasons
will "be remembered in history as someone who failed to save Israel."
That's a reference to any moves by Netanyahu who has alleged election fraud without evidence
and remains caretaker prime minister during this process.
Lauren Freya, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
The United Nations Climate Summit, known as COP 31, opens today in Turkey.
Thousands of diplomats, executives and world leaders are gathered in the Turkish Mediterranean
city of Antalya.
And PR's Hadil Al-Shelchi reports they're expected to discuss how nations must slash
greenhouse gas emissions.
This year's climate summit opens during a global energy crisis sparked by the U.S.-Israeli
war with Iran.
Experts say this makes the push to replace fossil fuels with renewables even more urgent.
Climate hurdles are steep, however, the U.N. says the world will surpass the 1.5-degree
warming limit and developing nations receive barely a fraction of the $300 billion the
U.N. says they need to adapt.
The U.S., one of the biggest emitters of climate-warming gases, will be absent from the summit for
a second year in a row.
In 2026, President Trump withdrew the U.S. from the Paris Agreement, the legally binding
treaty to limit global warming.
And the U.S. is set to soon leave the larger framework that organizes international climate
negotiations.
Hadil Al-Shelchi, NPR News, Antalya.
This is NPR.
Officials at the Big Tech computer chip maker Nvidia are investigating their own CEO.
They say Jensen Huang was the "target" of a foreign intelligence effort.
Published reports say Huang is suspected of having a romantic relationship with a woman
who is an alleged Chinese spy, and NPR has not confirmed this reporting.
Nvidia published a memo that Huang wrote to employees, where he admits and apologizes
for his role in the relationship.
Meanwhile, China is denying any role in the matter.
Devastating floods in southwest Colorado last week could not stop residents from voting
in the midterm elections.
This morning, a state-owned helicopter will fly ballots across the flood-ravaged section
of the state so they can be counted.
Colorado Public Radio's Steena Sieg has more.
The ballots were cast by Archuleta County residents, evacuated from their homes or cut
off from their typical voting center by historic flooding.
Many of them voted at a temporary center set up in neighboring La Plata County, where Tiffany
Lee is the clerk and recorder.
She will oversee about a hundred ballots being loaded onto a helicopter so they can be counted
in the correct county, even though they won't change outcomes.
It doesn't matter.
Those ballots still need to be counted, and those voters still need to have their voice
heard.
Even during a disaster, or maybe especially during one.
For NPR News, I'm Steena Sieg.
And I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News, from Washington.
